title: Have your AI call my AI
summary: Sharp lawyers have often used the fine print to win an advantage in a contract. It’s called the fine print for a reason–you’re not supposed to read it. But you should. Now, armed with AI, it’s significantly easier to bury arcane, unfair or unanticipated clauses in agreements, even (and especially) if we don’t expect it. […]
reason: Seth Godin on AI making it easier to hide unfair clauses in contracts, and why you'll need your own AI to read the fine print.
content_html:
Sharp lawyers have often used the fine print to win an advantage in a contract. It’s called the fine print for a reason–you’re not supposed to read it. But you should.

Now, armed with AI, it’s significantly easier to bury arcane, unfair or unanticipated clauses in agreements, even (and especially) if we don’t expect it.

You shouldn’t sign anything until you’ve had your AI read it. And if it’s important, have your lawyer and her AI read it too.

The next step seems reasonable to me: You and I describe our agreement in plain English and then our mutual AI’s work out a written agreement that actually captures what we’ve agreed on. And for the avoidance of doubt, append each AI’s interpretation to the contract itself.

It shouldn’t be confrontational or adversarial. After all, it’s an agreement.

title: Spend Your Boon
summary: Occasionally, some technical advancement arrives that gives us more time. Historically, these advances were hundreds of years apart. Now they come a lot quicker. Right now, we’re going through the disruption tumble dryer once again with the arrival of agentic AI. The upside to these things is that once we get our arms around the new thing, some things that used to take a lot of time now take very little. That gives us, in theory, extra time. In other words, a boon. A lot of us are getting our ar
reason: David Sparks on spending the time agentic AI gives back wisely, a thoughtful take on AI and how people work.
content_html:
Occasionally, some technical advancement arrives that gives us more time. Historically, these advances were hundreds of years apart. Now they come a lot quicker. Right now, we’re going through the disruption tumble dryer once again with the arrival of agentic AI.

The upside to these things is that once we get our arms around the new thing, some things that used to take a lot of time now take very little. That gives us, in theory, extra time.

In other words, a boon.

A lot of us are getting our arms around AI now to actually start realizing that boon. I am! I don’t know how this whole AI thing is going to shake out, but I can’t deny AI’s taken a lot of donkey work off my plate.

The question is how we spend that boon.

When we talk about getting time back, we all give lip service to the idea of spending it on ourselves. Because in our heads, that quality-of-life moment is always just around the corner, right up until the moment they put you in a box.

But too often, what we actually do is the opposite. We look at our increased capacity and take on more work. The space opens up, and we immediately fill it by putting more on our backs.

At the end of the day, we’ve gained productivity and lost quality of life. Somehow, the boon that was supposed to give us breathing room has left us with even more to do. This keeps happening to us all.

This time, I’m actively trying to spend the boon on myself.

I’m using my AI boon to become more analog. By that, I mean more time in the woodshop, in the garden, reading books, taking care of myself, and spending time with my family.

Those are the things I want the extra time for. I want to get the necessary work done and then go touch grass.

This is a lot more difficult than it sounds.

These technology jumps are like catnip to me. The more I play with them, the deeper I want to go. I get one thing working and immediately see three more things I could get it to do. Before long, I’m spending the afternoon investigating how to save myself an afternoon.

And even when the technology does save me time, there’s still that temptation to fill the space with more work. I could make more content or take on another thing. After all, things are fun.

This time, however, I’m not ensnaring myself. I’m making a sincere effort to let the saved time stay mine. I want my AI boon to be a particularly well-built cabinet or a trip with my wife.

How about you? Have you thought about how you’ll spend your boon?

As these tools become more capable, we will all have opportunities to make this choice. If we don’t think about it, we’ll fall right into that more-at-the-grindstone trap.

So when something gives you an hour back, decide where you want that hour to go.

Don’t squander your boon.

The post Spend Your Boon appeared first on MacSparky.

title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
summary: On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that […]
reason: A Verge feature on Jensen Huang and the fading era of showman founder CEOs, good leadership and industry analysis.
content_html:
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.

Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO

The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.﻿

Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang Unveils New Innovations At CES 2025

Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang Unveils New Innovations At CES 2025

Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.

The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.

The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.

It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.

“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.

But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.

“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.

Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.

Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.

I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.

But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.

His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot.

What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.

In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.

He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC.

Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.

“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”

“NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla.

“Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me.

It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value.

But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge.

That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution.

Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.

But that bet on ARM-based phone chips did put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022 Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs to handle the load.

“Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”

“Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”

As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit every single second! — and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024, The Wall Street Journal and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including one on a woman’s chest.

In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions.

It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous “reality distortion field” at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity.

But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone. Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world. The question now is: who for Nvidia?

“He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the blame.”

Does Nvidia work without Huang?

Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet.

“This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.”

“Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.”

“He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says IDC analyst Tom Mainelli. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him will be key, and there will undoubtedly be bumps along the way. But the company will survive.”

“Jensen built an exceptionally talented organization with a deep engineering bench, a mature, heavily-resourced software ecosystem, and strong customer relationships,” says Dave Altavilla, HotTech Vision and Analysis. “His departure undoubtedly leaves a leadership and strategic vision gap, but the technology, talent, and execution capabilities he helped establish aren’t going away. The real question is whether his successor can sustain that same long-term vision and willingness to invest ahead of the market.”

“No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” says Jon Peddie of Jon Peddie Research. “Whoever that is will not be Jensen, won’t have the same ambitions, the same contacts and relationships, the same vision, or the same courage to make big, long-term bets. We’ve seen this in Apple, AMD, Intel, and other companies. So the stock will probably get battered around a bit until investors see some stability and fewer ‘what if’ questions.”

content_html:
Have you felt lightheaded during the past day?  

Perhaps you should have, because the atmospheric pressure has been unusually low.

Low enough to cause a significant rise in sea level.

Consider a plot of sea-level pressure for SeaTac Airport since July (below).  The pressure dropped to 990 hPa, the lowest observed during the period, by a LOT.


Our extremely low pressure was associated with a deep low-pressure center immediately to our west (see the analysis at 4 AM Friday).   At this time, the low center had a central pressure of 968 hPa, which is low for this latitude.


The average pressure for Seattle in November is 1017 hPa (the average around the nation is 1013 hPa), so our pressure on Friday was 27 hPa below normal.

Localized low pressure causes sea level to rise by approximately 1 cm for every decline of 1 hPa.  (See schematic below).


Thus, sea level over Seattle was elevated by 27 cm or 10.6 inches by the low pressure.  Almost a foot!

You want to see the low pressure in action on sea level?   

Below is a plot below of predicted (blue) versus observed (red) sea level in Seattle.   The difference between the two has increased this week as the low-pressure center approached, with sea level 2.2 feet above normal.  



So about 40% of the anomalous sea level rise was due to the low pressure.

But the effects of the low center on sea level do not end there.

The low center is associated with powerful westerly (from the west) and southwesterly winds (see forecast surface winds at 1 PM Friday below).   Winds near the coast were strongly from the south (southerly)


Such southerly winds push on the ocean surface, which flows TOWARDS the coast by the Coriolis force, resulting in a HIGHER water level.  See schematic below of this situation.  Want to impress your friends?  This is called Ekman Transport.

But the high water fun caused by the low center does not end there!

The offshore low with strong winds over a large area (long fetch) produces big waves that can bring the water levels up even more on the coast (see forecast wave heights for Friday morning below).

There are other, more minor contributors to short-term high water levels, such as a Kelvin wave associated with the El Nino moving up the coast (several inches).     

The good news is that water levels should drop as the low center weakens over the weekend.

title: A Most Perfect iPad
summary: The new OLED iPad mini feels nearly flawless...
reason: Kafka's review of the new OLED iPad mini from a favorite writer.
content_html:
Ever since the very first version, I've been a huge fan of the iPad mini. Apple took the iPad itself and distilled it down to a far more wieldable touchscreen device. This was a time before iPhone screens were massive. For certain tasks, it seemed like the perfect portable computer. And with the latest version Apple has just released, I think they've perfected the iPad line they originally set out to create.

That last bit is important because it calls back to Apple's own vision for the device. And it allows me to make such a statement without needing to acknowledge that the software still leaves quite a bit to be desired. Because Apple never wanted this to be a "big iPhone" and certainly not a "mini Mac", it has existed in this sort of in-between state for many tasks. And that's fine – again, I'm a huge fan. And yes, I think this is the best version of that vision. Perhaps the best possible.

And it comes at an interesting and perhaps perfect time, at least for the mini. While the aforementioned growing iPhone screens have long called into question the need for the smaller iPad, now the iPhone Duo kicks that debate into hyperdrive. No, they're not the same thing, but when the Duo is unfolded, they are fairly similar in size. Similar enough that it's unreasonable to think that people would buy both. I mean I did, but I'm crazy. But even I can't imagine regularly carrying around both at the same time. It's 7" to 8" screen size overkill.1

Of course, it must be pointed out that one device starts at $699 while the other starts at $1,999. The latter is a high enough price point that it's reasonable to think that the iPad mini can still have a nice, long life from here as the majority of consumers won't be buying the foldable iPhone at that price point any time soon.

But would they buy an iPad mini when there is also a cheaper iPad with a larger screen (the $449 "regular" iPad with an 11" screen)? That's a fair question, one Apple made a little harder with the recent price hikes. Then again, if you're at all partial to a smaller iPad, this new mini – with a top-of-the-line A20 Pro chip – will also be far more powerful than the cheaper iPad variant.

It's so fast that it's almost, dare I say, an iPad Pro mini. Yes, yes there's no ProMotion (read: better refresh rates), which is a bit weird, but also not a big deal in my usage. Bigger is the inclusion of an OLED screen at last. Again, this almost feels like Apple checking the last few remaining boxes to perfect the device.

Speeds and feeds aside, what strikes me about this new iPad mini is just how striking it is. From a pure hardware perspective, it's gorgeous. Certainly the best-looking iPad ever, and one of the most beautiful Apple products ever, period. It's so sleek and slick. The new placement of the speaker behind the screen (wild how well this works) means the removal of the speaker holes. And that makes for a device that looks and feels literally seamless.

This seemingly airtight machine also allows it to be water resistant for the first time. Again, more boxes checked. Speaking of, the bezels have also now shrunk a bit, and while you might think an edge-to-edge screen would be one obvious thing yet to come, it's not clear how you would comfortably hold such a device without obscuring part of the screen. Again, it seems pretty perfected right now...

And at ever-so-slightly more than a half a pound in weight (technically 0.56 pounds), and 0.21" in depth, it's hard to imagine how Apple could possibly shave more weight and depth off of this device. Incidentally, it's the exact same weight as the iPhone Duo – but because that device is often folded and as such, smaller, that feels far heavier, as many reviewers (including myself) have noted.2 The 0.56 pounds spread over a 7.69" by 5.22" frame makes it feel almost like holding an empty shell. It's wild just how light it feels to walk around with when holding in your hands. And while yes, you could fit in in a large pocket, the iPhone Duo is always going to have an edge there...

I opted for the "nano-texture" (read: matte) display which is an option (read: an extra $100) on the higher-end (read: higher storage) models.3 This also makes it match that inner screen of the iPhone Duo, with uses the matte finish to help hide the crease. The iPad mini, of course, has no such obfuscation needs, so you don't need the nano-texture. I simply prefer both the look and feel. And because I anticipate using the device outdoors, perhaps near pools especially with said water resistance, which is admittedly more aspirational as it's current literally freezing in London at the moment with a sun that sets around 4pm.

Anyway, I hope Apple keeps making the iPad mini. There were one or two times in the past when it seemed like it was going away in a world of those aforementioned ever-larger iPhones, yet it has somehow lingered long enough to now reach this new pinnacle. It would be a fitting end if the Duo eventually does it in. But again, there's hope in that price gap alone, which may make that moment years away still.

For now, this is simply the iPad, perfected.

One more thing: as I noted in my iPhone Duo thoughts, another subtle, but interesting difference between using the Duo versus the iPad mini despite the similar screen sizes is the inclination to use the former horizontally (the natural orientation when you unfold it) while using the latter vertically (the natural orientation when you open the cover). And with the iOS design tweaks for the Duo, it's clearly built for that horizontal usage, while accommodating the vertical, versus vice versa.

By the way, the new "TechWoven" case is a fantastic change from the old polyurethane variety. It feels much more like carrying around an actual nice notebook now, albeit an insanely thin one. It also changes the way it you use the cases to prop up the iPad mini, with magnets in the case now cleverly providing a couple different viewing angles. And yes, it pairs beautifully with the iPhone Duo TechWoven Folio...

1 And yes, there's bleed into the iPhone Pro Max screen size as well, at 6.9". ↩

2 Fine, technically it's one gram heavier. Really a single gram separates the two! The WiFi version of the iPad mini, at least. ↩

3 Perhaps this helps solve the Duo dilemma for some: if you want a non-matte screen on a 7" to 8" Apple device, the non-nano-texture iPad mini may be fore you! ↩

title: Cursor Says Stolen Fireworks AI Key Led to Trojanized Claude Code Extension Incident
summary: The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said in a Friday update. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only
reason: A stolen key led to a trojanized Claude Code extension, a real supply chain and key management lesson.
content_html:
The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI.

"An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said in a Friday update. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them."

The disclosure comes nearly two weeks after a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate update, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems.

According to the artificial intelligence (AI)-powered coding platform, the read-only storage bucket is said to have contained limited coding agent traces from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode. Privacy Mode is a Cursor-specific setting that, if enabled, allows users to opt out of their data being used for training purposes.

These sessions, most of which date back to 2025, were permitted to be used for model training. Among these traces were credentials that had not been edited out, exposing the API credentials of less than 0.01% of customers in the process.

The attacker, Cursor added, used these credentials as a starting point to reach select software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools used by Cursor and then access the following data -

  • Select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories, including some containing business contact information
  • Limited customer support data and email conversations
  • Product usage metrics and contact details
  • Summaries of some coding agent conversations
  • Some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team

Cursor said it took steps to deactivate the vendor's key, revoke and rotate credentials, and hunt for signs of deeper access, and contain it after "we identified further access." The company also said it temporarily disabled internal and product services, disrupting access to some Cursor features.

The next phase of the attack took place on October 29, 2026, when the attacker used a stolen credential from the exposed data of its internal system to place trojanized versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve Cursor's extension marketplace.

"At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build," Cursor said. "It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down."

The company said it notified affected users who installed versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the marketplace during the exposure window and helped revoke exposed credentials. It has also moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, deactivated the key issued to it, and cut off its access to all data sets we shared with it.

Furthermore, Cursor emphasized that no additional malicious activity has been detected since November 1, 2026.

There is no evidence that the incident impacted users who had enabled Privacy Mode, customer code repositories, Cursor's own production environment, Cursor app and its official updates, its other apps, or any other extension or plugin downloaded from Cursor Marketplace.

Uber Also Impacted by Fireworks Incident

The development comes as Uber confirmed unknown threat actors stole thousands of drivers' license information after obtaining internal credentials.

"On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third-party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," the company said in a filing with the U.S. state of California. "On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider."

Although the name of the provider was not disclosed, TechCrunch reported that the provider in question is Fireworks AI. Uber has not disclosed how many users were impacted by the breach. Last week, online productivity startup Notion also confirmed its data was stolen in the Fireworks AI hack.

content_html:
Patrick McGee (author of Apple in China; my guest on The Talk Show last May), writing on X in response to Semafor’s reporting that Nvidia is “considering” Johny Srouji:

Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji would be an incredible choice to lead @nvidia — and I believe he’d accept it.

He’s hit the ceiling at Apple and won’t ever be CEO; obviously competent; ambitious as hell; has long wanted chip designs to dictate Apple product launches/timelines.

I wrote about this a few days ago, that my money is on Srouji having no interest in the Nvidia job. It’s true that Srouji will almost certainly never be CEO at Apple. But it’s wrong to assume that Srouji would consider CEO of Nvidia to be an upgrade from CHO at Apple. There’s no way Eddy Cue, Craig Federighi, or Greg Joswiak would leave Apple to be CEO at another company. Most of Apple’s leadership genuinely bleeds six colors. There’s a certain approach to product that drives them, motivates them, and literally only Apple does that type of work. Tim Cook surely turned down numerous CEO offers to leave Apple while he served as COO under Steve Jobs, and he’s always been clear that he hoped Jobs would stay a few steps ahead of his cancer and could remain at Apple until, well, probably around now. (Jobs would be 71.)

I’ve never met Srouji and don’t have a read on him like I do other leaders at Apple. But I do have a read on Ternus and Cook. I’ll stick with my bet from earlier in the week:

Another scenario is that Srouji meant what he said, loves his job at Apple, and truly is John Ternus’s trusted and trustworthy hardware lieutenant. In this case, Nvidia’s board leaking that they’re considering Srouji to replace Huang is like someone in hell saying they’re considering ordering some ice water.

Aside from Srouji’s loyalty to Apple (and to the Apple Silicon chip architecture that’s been his life’s work), there’s also the question of whether he’d take the gig at Nvidia in particular, even if he is open to leaving Apple. Jensen Huang has left the company with a $4 trillion market cap, yes, but it was $5 trillion just a week ago. It now seems 20 percent of Nvidia’s sales in the AI era have been in violation of U.S. national security export controls to China. The company has no internal leadership hierarchy. And Huang placed bets that have leveraged the company’s future on OpenAI and the overall data center mania not being a bubble. Srouji has been a senior leader at the one tech company that conspicuously avoided those bets entirely.

title: Confusion about causation
summary: It’s not difficult to develop an incorrect theory. Ice cream and spaghetti have more letters than tofu and celery, so therefore, foods with long names are more fattening than those with short ones. If you start moving forward with this theory, you’ll soon find outliers. Sugar only has five letters, and watercress has ten. If […]
reason: A short Seth Godin lesson on bad causal theories, useful for any PM reading data.
content_html:
It’s not difficult to develop an incorrect theory. Ice cream and spaghetti have more letters than tofu and celery, so therefore, foods with long names are more fattening than those with short ones.

If you start moving forward with this theory, you’ll soon find outliers. Sugar only has five letters, and watercress has ten. If we want to stick with our theory, we’ll have to come up with more and more complex reasons why we ignore some of the data and embrace the rest.

Of course, this is absurd.

And yet we do it all the time. Ornate explanations about the stock market, SEO or politics. Charts and graphs where we spend most of our time fitting a plot to a few dots, or amplifying the obscure to justify the theory.

A simple theory that matches the data is much more likely to accurately explain causation. It might not be a comfortable theory, or one that matches our trajectory, but it’s a better theory.

It turns out that the number of letters is completely irrelevant to how fattening a food is. I’m sorry you spent all this time on research, but you’re on the wrong path.

If you want to know why your marketing, your investments or your arguments are floundering, it might pay to reconsider the theory, not look for more data to justify the current one.

SpaceX captured Starship using the arms of ‘Mechazilla’ its launch and catch tower for the first time.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.

title: Siri AI and iPhone apps are the cornerstones of Apple’s hardware strategy
summary: Earlier this month, Apple rolled out its Siri AI Developer Preview, which lays the groundwork for developers to allow their apps to be controlled in a fairly sophisticated fashion by Apple’s AI assistant.…
reason: Snell analysis of how Siri AI and apps anchor Apple hardware strategy, a favorites-style piece.
content_html:
Earlier this month, Apple rolled out its Siri AI Developer Preview, which lays the groundwork for developers to allow their apps to be controlled in a fairly sophisticated fashion by Apple’s AI assistant.

To say this is an important development would be a colossal understatement. The execution of this feature is the core of Apple’s game plan for the next few years, when it intends to release numerous products that leverage its iPhone app ecosystem to power Siri AI.

No pressure…

Apple’s latest new product, the HomeView, is built around Siri AI. (It’s a light dash of Siri AI right now, but its links with content on individual iPhones show what the company is envisioning there.) The new Apple TV 4K has added microphones to make it an additional home access point for Siri AI.

And there’s much more to come, as reported by Mark Gurman at Bloomberg:

Apple needs software makers to begin preparing for what it hopes will be its flagship new product of 2027: smart glasses built around Siri AI, code-named N50.

Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses, I’m told. The idea is to make those apps available through Siri, allowing users to get things done without grabbing their phones. Apple believes its large developer ecosystem could give it an advantage over Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google, potentially providing countless third-party integrations when the glasses go on sale.

Gurman expects the Siri-powered glasses (which are basically AirPods you wear on your face) to be released at WWDC, with a similar set of AirPods armed with AI-powered cameras set to debut later in the year. (We’ll see.)

These devices don’t make a lot of sense unless there’s a useful AI assistant behind them. Siri AI is not quite that yet—it’s more reliable and more useful than the old Siri was, but it’s not as good as it should be, and it’s sometimes very slow—but at least it’s promising. Still, just as the iPhone would be a lot less appealing if it only ran Apple-built apps, Siri AI is less appealing if it doesn’t have access to the functionality of the app ecosystem.

Currently, Siri AI can use Spotlight to search content offered by third-party apps, but what it can’t do is learn about functionality offered by individual apps and command those apps to perform those functions in service of a larger request. That’s the goal of the Siri AI Developer Preview—and that sort of stuff is what’s going to make the HomeView (let alone glasses or AirPods paired with an iPhone) a more appealing product.

If Apple can’t pull this off, well, it calls into question the trajectory of Apple’s entire future product strategy. There’s no point in making amazing hardware if there’s nothing running on it that appeals.

title: Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches
summary: Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs)
reason: Google reports attackers using autonomous AI agents to turn patches into exploits, relevant to security engineering.
content_html:
Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.

The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same.

A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China.

"These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said.

Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation.

"Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added.

Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers.

The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines.

This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so.

"The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

Google News,

content_html:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled ​“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”​ As I explained:

“To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote ​several​ ​more​ ​essays​ on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I ​launched my podcast​, I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, ​The Deep Life: A Structured Approach​, is now ​available for pre-order​.

The Deep Life brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend ​Oliver Burkeman​, to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

“It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is the key that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

  • ​Amazon​
  • ​Barnes & Noble​
  • ​Bookshop.org​
  • ​Amazon UK​
  • ​Waterstones ​

You can also pre-order ​a signed copy​ from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. Why not make it deep?

The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport.

content_html:
Apple is urging Canada to change a proposed law that it says could weaken the privacy and security protections built into its products.


The legislation, Bill C-22, is intended to help police and intelligence agencies obtain digital information during investigations. According to Bloomberg, Apple, Google, and Meta are lobbying for changes as Canadian senators review the bill.

At the center of the dispute is whether companies could be forced to change how their services work to help authorities access user data. The bill would allow the government to require companies to build tools for that purpose, with approval from Canada's Intelligence Commissioner.

It could also require certain providers to keep records about users' connections for up to six months. This metadata would exclude the contents of messages, browsing history, and social media activities.

Lawmakers have already added safeguards. For example, a company could only be required to unlock encrypted data if it supplied the encryption and already has the information needed to unlock it. The bill also says companies cannot be forced to introduce certain security weaknesses into their services.

Apple says those changes do not fully address its concerns. The company welcomed the government's revisions, but told Bloomberg that the bill would still undermine its ability to protect users' data. Apple previously warned that the legislation could let authorities demand backdoors.

Meta, Signal, and Tailscale representatives are scheduled to appear before a Senate committee today. The bill has not yet become law.

I wrote about David Sacks the other day, in the context of his being one of the Trump 2.0 gang that might get left holding the bag if this Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal blows up the AI boom/bubble. Sacks was the administration’s “AI czar” — until March, when he announced his time was up. (His position as a “special government employee” was limited to 130 days. Sacks is definitely special.)

At the moment Sacks remains co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST), a Legion of Doom-style committee of billionaire Trump backers, whose members include, in alphabetical order after the co-chairs:

  • David Sacks — Co-chair
  • Michael Kratsios — Co-chair
  • Marc Andreessen (Andreessen Horowitz)
  • Pam Bondi (fired as Trump attorney general for insufficient cravenness, no background whatsoever in science or technology)
  • Sergey Brin (Google)
  • Safra Catz (Oracle)
  • Michael Dell (Dell Technologies)
  • Jacob DeWitte (Oklo — nuclear power startup, fission)
  • Fred Ehrsam (Coinbase — crypto)
  • Larry Ellison (Oracle)
  • David Friedberg (Ohalo — biotech)
  • Jensen Huang (Nvidia)
  • John Martinis (Qolab — quantum computing)
  • Bob Mumgaard (Commonwealth Fusion Systems — nuclear power, fusion)
  • Lisa Su (AMD)
  • Mark Zuckerberg (Meta)

Not represented: anyone from Apple, Microsoft, or Amazon. There’s a game of reverse musical chairs here, and, amongst the multi-trillion-dollar tech Goliaths, it’s Nvidia, Google, and Meta who are still sitting in seats, soaking up the stench of a historically unpopular president — whose unpopularity is fueled first and foremost, according to election exit polls, by his abject corruption. Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon have seemingly made their Irish goodbyes. Being associated with Trump now doesn’t just put you on the wrong side of popular party politics, but on the wrong side of being perceived as crooked.

Curiously absent from PCAST is Elon Musk, who I think got his licks in all at once with the DOGE fiasco in Trump 2.0’s first year.

title: Jensen Huang, as Told By His Biographer
summary: An interview with Stephen Witt
reason: Pogue interview with Huang biographer amid the Nvidia CEO news.
content_html:
Jensen Huang has landed himself in a honeypot of hot water.

Huang is the founder of Nvidia, the company that makes virtually all of the computers used to power the AI explosion, and the world’s biggest company (by stock value). Turns out he’s also a serial cheater on his wife. Most recently, he slept with a suspected Chinese spy, in what seems to be a honeypot operation. That’s why he’s now the ex-CEO of Nvidia.

Few people have followed Jensen Huang more closely than journalist Steven Witt. His book about Huang, The Thinking Machine, came out last year—and is suddenly a hot seller again.

In late April, I interviewed Witt for a “CBS Sunday Morning” story that never aired. This conversation took place, of course, before Huang’s dramatic downfall. Part of the fun of reading this excerpt of our interview is the parts that did, and did not, age well. (Here’s Witt’s update, which appeared in The New York Times this week.)

What he’s like

POGUE: You’ve gotten to know Jensen through a series of interviews. What is he actually like?

WITT: One of his executives compared interacting with Jensen to sticking your finger into an electrical socket. (laughs) That is accurate. That is what it is like to talk to Jensen. I mean, he is so intense. He’s so smart. He’s so tightly wound.

He can be hard to follow. Sometimes he says things that don’t seem to make much sense. And often he contradicts himself.

I was talking to one of his friends, and he said, “Look, you have to understand, Jensen is not a politician. He’s not trying to stay on message. He’s thinking out loud. And if he contradicts himself, it’s because he has a new thought that occurred to him just in that moment, and he’s just articulating it for the first time.”

So often you will see Jensen kind of almost, like, auditioning new ideas or material, even in an interview setting. With Jensen, there’s no attempt to hide the real Jensen from the media.

It’s a very rare quality in a CEO. He’ll tell you exactly what he’s thinking right at that second. That almost never happens with corporate management. It’s actually very refreshing. And this is my favorite thing about Jensen.

POGUE: (LAUGHS) There is this tech-CEO thing that has happened in the last few years to Bezos and Zuckerberg, where they turn from good guys, with progressive values and some empathy for the public, into these sort of Trump-worshiping muscle men with some less pleasant aspects of their personalities. Jensen seems like, in general, he’s one of the last tech billionaire good guys.

WITT: Yeah. So I think what happened is that—and this happens a lot in men—those guys are going through a midlife crisis. Jensen already went through that. Remember, Jensen is older than these guys. And Nvidia and AI did not really take off until he was 50 years old.

Jensen actually had his weightlifting phase way back in the late 2000s, back in the video game days. You can watch him getting progressively more swole, and he didn’t always wear the leather jacket. He used to dress like a dork. That was a makeover that came when he was like 50 years old, right?

So he already went through that phase.

And look, Jensen has his masculine side. He likes whiskey. He likes sports cars. He rolled a sports car once, in the grand Silicon Valley tradition. (LAUGHS) But he’s a little more mature than those guys. I think he’s been through that already and has come out the other side.

Also, he really is a family man.

You know, he’s not—he’s not Elon Musk. He doesn’t have, you know, 14 children by surrogates. Like, he is a family guy. Both of his kids work at Nvidia.

He has elements of Steve Jobs. He has elements of Elon Musk. But he is his own guy. He’s his own person. And in the future, when we’re talking about the next Silicon Valley executive, we’ll say, “This guy has a little Jensen in him.”

The temper

POGUE: You’ve also written very colorfully about his temper, his habit of dressing down employees. Can you square that with Nvidia being called one of the best places to work, and employees staying for decades?

WITT: Yeah. So Jensen has a terrible temper. He can scream at employees for hours. And typically, he will do so in a public setting. So he’ll make you stand up in front of 20 and 30 people and just chew you out for 60 minutes nonstop.

And not only is he yelling, he can be really mean. He can say some really mean, cutting stuff to people. Like, insults. And because the insults are sort of accurate, they really hit home and they hurt your feelings.

And yet, Nvidia has a reputation as one of the best places to work. So why is that? Well, first of all, Nvidia is a generous employer. And in particular, they’re generous with stock options. I read that 50% of Nvidia employees have a net worth above $25 million. So if you’re at the company, you have so much money that you’re gonna put up with this guy yelling at you.

One employee described working at Nvidia to me as “the Olympics of suffering.” There is a corporate culture of just dedicating everything to the company, every waking moment of your life to the company. You’re working all the time.

You know, the boss will yell at you, yes. But you have a lot of freedom actually to pursue what you wanna do, as long as you’re showing the drive that Jensen wants to see.

There’s a cult-leader aspect to Jensen. He’s like a prophet who makes predictions about the future. But the difference between Jensen and most prophets, and most cult leaders, is the things that Jensen says are gonna happen actually do happen, and this makes people love him.

The other thing: these are the best engineers alive. They are some of the smartest people out there. Their life’s mission to work on cutting-edge, futuristic technology—and this is the most cutting-edge, futuristic technology in the world. It’s some of the most important technology ever. So these engineers, they know that they are writing their names into the history of computing, maybe even the history of humanity.

So the fear of missing out that they would get from not being at Nvidia is quite high, and this actually transcends money. It’s purpose.

Trump

POGUE: What’s his relationship to the Trump Administration?

WITT: Jensen has gotten close to Trump. They’ve appeared in public seven times together in the past year. He seems to like Trump personally. He went on “Joe Rogan” and praised aspects of Trump’s genius. And Nvidia is funding the East Wing Ballroom, at least in part.

And Jensen has gotten what he wants from Trump, which is to get that ban on sales of semiconductor equipment to China lifted. That was not what the U.S. national security establishment wanted. They do not want Nvidia to sell its chips to China. But Jensen has managed to convince Trump that it’s a good idea.

You know, Trump listens to Jensen. I think Trump listens to Jensen more than he listens to any other Silicon Valley executive. If you were to do a Silicon Valley power ranking, Jensen would be number one.

At the same time, California has this billionaires tax that has been proposed. Almost everyone in Silicon Valley is against this tax, except Jensen. He seems to think that there should be a tax on billionaires. [Update: Voters rejected the proposal.]

You know, Jensen’s not an ideological character. He’s neither Republican nor a Democrat; he’s an engineer. And he’s gonna approach each political problem not through the realm of ideology, but through the realm of engineering. “What is the problem to be solved? What are the inputs that I modify to solve that problem? And what are the outputs of that result?”

AI bubble

POGUE: We hear these days about the possibility of an AI bubble, that all this investment is unsustainably too much.

WITT: I don’t think it’s a bubble. You know, Nvidia’s valuation is not that extreme, given their size. It’s not. This doesn’t look like the dot-com bubble to me. This doesn’t have the same stupidity and froth as some of the stuff we saw in the past.

This seems more like the invention of the railroads in the 19th century.

Now, the railroads transformed the American economy, but there were still speculative bubbles associated with the railroads. So it can certainly be the case that AI lives up the promise and is still a bubble. That’s what makes it hard to predict.

The question to me is, A, are people gonna use this stuff? Do they want AI products? And B, are we gonna hit some plateau where suddenly we can’t push AI any further, and then suddenly demand for Jensen’s microchips collapses? That could also happen.

I don’t think we’re in a bubble. That doesn’t mean Nvidia’s stock price can’t go down. I can’t predict the future. But I don’t see the kind of insanity that I would normally associate with a bubble here.

Nvidia stock

POGUE: How dependent is the average person’s finances on Nvidia continuing to do well as a stock?

WITT: Much more than the average person realizes. So Nvidia is about 7-8% of the S&P 500. Companies affiliated with Nvidia are even more, like Microsoft. Microsoft is all the data centers running Nvidia equipment.

So it’s all bundled together. Ultimately, if Americans want to retire comfortably, Nvidia has to succeed. AI has to succeed. As an economy, we’re all in on this bet, right? And if for some reason it doesn’t work, the stock market will collapse.

Jensen’s power

POGUE: Would you say that Jensen’s strengths are greater as an engineer or as a businessman?

WITT: He’s an engineer. The reason he’s a good businessman is ‘cause he has engineered himself to be that. Jensen does not have an MBA. He has a master’s in electrical engineering from Stanford University. He is an engineer to the core.

The way he thinks about problems, even business problems, is: he breaks them down like an engineer into their components, into their inputs and outputs, and then modifies the inputs to get the outputs that he wants.

Do not get me wrong. He’s an excellent, excellent businessman. He is the best businessman maybe alive. But at his core, the way he thinks about problems, he is an engineer.

POGUE: Where does he rank in the world in terms of power?

WITT: Jensen is the single-most powerful person in AI. So that’s very powerful. Trump’s gonna get voted out of office eventually. He’s gotta go some point. But no one’s getting rid of Jensen.

title: Don’t put all your eggs in one city
summary: Sichuan and the Sun Belt
reason: Works in Progress piece on city concentration and resilience.
content_html:
Dan Wang explores why America and China both draw their strength from many rival cities, not one dominant capital.

This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print. If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here.

Vienna has five times more people than Graz, Austria’s second city. London is four times, Seoul six times, and Paris seven times larger than their countries’ next largest cities. These primate cities are the singular political, cultural, and financial centers of their countries, hosting the overwhelming concentration of the national elite.

Washington, DC and Beijing are awesomely powerful entities. Yet Beijing is not China’s largest city – that’s Shanghai – while DC does not rank among even the top five metro areas of the United States. The political center of both countries sometimes struggles to assert itself against other national hubs. That tension imbues the United States and China with productive friction. It is part of the reason that they are superpowers that have been able to combine social dynamism with jealous states.

Earlier this summer, I visited a few comedy shows in Shanghai. Performers have to submit their scripts beforehand so that censors can expurgate any routine that carries a whiff of political commentary. But they will permit jokes on regional stereotypes. I listened to stand-up comedians make fun of Shanghainese, who worship money while henpecked husbands are governed by formidable women. I heard them say that folks from Liaoning and other northeastern provinces became conniving drunks after the local economy collapsed, but they are redeemed by humor and loyalty. Everyone appreciated the idea that people in the northern metropolis of Beijing can hold forth beautifully on any topic – though that is all they can do.

Subscribe now

This comedy reveals a deeper point: China is made up of distinctive macro regions. China’s central government has for millennia tried to impose its will on the entire nation. Though top leader Xi Jinping wields more governance instruments than any former emperor, central authorities still have to contend with the ambitions of different regions. New investments do not end up in Beijing by default. They also go toward the southwestern mountain zone centered around Sichuan and Chongqing, the coastal provinces of Fujian and Guangdong, the populous heartland of Hubei and Hunan, and around a half dozen other macro zones.

Usable Security at Luxury Hotels

Interesting case study from luxury hotels. Attackers used a fake booking request to gain access to a reservations inbox, where they copied genuine refund requests and got fraudulent ones approved.

This is a good illustration why “just don’t click on links” is bad advice. It can’t work when answering strangers’ emails is the job. And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer.

title: Practical empathy
summary: I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe. And that’s okay. In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen. Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and […]
reason: Seth Godin on empathy, close to his favorited posts.
content_html:
I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe.

And that’s okay.

In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen.

Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and our approach than anyone else. We have a noise in our head, a narrative and a point of view we’ve spent our whole lives creating. It’s naive to believe that anyone else is completely in sync with us.

And so, our only opportunity is to go where they are, not to demand that they come to us.

Practical empathy isn’t primarily an act of kindness (though it’s an essential component of kindness.) Instead, it’s a direct and straightforward path from here to there. It’s how we create action, learning and change.

Marketing is the simple and brave act of going to where someone else might be, and helping them get to where they hope to go.

reason: Engineering post-mortem of how one bad router hurt air traffic control.
content_html:
Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong.

America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router

Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.﻿

America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router

Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.﻿

A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn’t offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights.

For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn’t be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician and rest in their own bed. First, they had to connect through Atlanta.

“It was honestly pretty scary,” Khera said. “We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”

“We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”

— Amanda Khera

She had every right to be scared. She didn’t know what was going on in the cockpit or on the ground. She had no idea that pilots are trained to follow strict procedures that minimize safety risks during major air traffic control outages. All she knew was that several recent incidents, including a midair collision over Reagan National Airport in 2025 that killed 67 people, have called into question the safety of America’s skies. So she spent the rest of the descent looking out the window for nearby aircraft.

Her flight landed safely. But she deplaned into a terminal frozen in place. More than 600 flights out of Atlanta, including their connection to Norfolk, had been canceled. And no one knew when they would be able to take off because every flight across the United States had been grounded.

On Friday, November 13, the nation’s air traffic control system began to fail. Around 3:15PM ET, pilots and air traffic controllers in the Midwest started reporting difficulty communicating with each other over the radio.

“We’re 11,000 [feet] over Grand Rapids airport, about nine miles to the west,” said the pilot of Allegiant Flight 547, his transmission already becoming garbled. “Unable to get… contact… approach on any [frequency].”

Four minutes later, controllers at Quad Cities Airport in Moline, Illinois, reported similar issues across the region.

“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated,” said one. “It sounds like Chicago Approach is going ATC zero, so it might be worse than we initially thought. We thought it was just here.”

With communication outages spreading around the country, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” From that moment on, no airplanes were allowed to take off in US airspace.

The sudden halt surprised both pilots and controllers.

“Just a heads up, we went in a national ground stop,” said a controller in Seattle.

“Are you saying national as in Reagan National,” asked one United pilot, “or national in the whole country?”

“Across all en route facilities, they’re having communication issues.”

Like so many of the safety incidents that have plagued the air traffic control system over the last few years, this latest failure began with a fragile and outdated piece of FAA infrastructure. In this case, according to the agency, the faulty system was the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI.

Built by defense giant L3Harris in the early 2000s, FTI is the data backbone of the entire air traffic control system. It links more than 4,400 aviation facilities and carries the voice and radar data controllers rely on to keep planes separated, bridging the gap between the FAA’s legacy phone-based transmission systems and modern Internet Protocol-based ones.

FTI is scheduled to be replaced in 2028. Until then, L3Harris must make incremental upgrades to keep FTI operational.

“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated.”

— Air traffic controller

One of these upgrades accidentally brought down the entire system, according to The Wall Street Journal. Early in the day, L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Once activated, however, the router began to flood the network with hundreds of connection attempts every second.

This may have added enough extra load to the system to degrade the whole network’s performance, according to I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University.

Hou explained that telecom networks break pieces of information — radio transmissions or radar coordinates, for example — into data packets small enough to be transmitted over the network and reassembled at the other end.

“When the network is degraded, it may start to lose a small portion of packets,” Hou says. “Since you need all packets to reassemble the data feed, just dropping one out of 10 packets may cause your feed to completely stop.”

Most modern communications apps are built to compensate for packet loss. FaceTime, for example, will blur the video or switch to audio-only to preserve the connection.

Air traffic control doesn’t have that luxury.

“Many NAS [National Air Space] applications … require a highly reliable synchronization source with exceptional stability,” according to FAA technical documentation, which warns that instability may cause widespread failure of critical systems.

FAA technicians believe the El Dorado router’s repeated connection attempts created enough instability within the FTI to cut off radio and radar feeds to 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and several Terminal Radar Approach Controls.

“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on,” Hou says.

“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on.”

— I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University

L3Harris’s contractors isolated the malfunctioning router and another one at a nearby radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Once those two routers were taken offline, the network began to stabilize once again.

Four and a half hours later, at 8:15PM ET, the FAA lifted the ground stop. It was the nation’s longest since 9/11, spurring airlines to cancel more than 13,000 flights and delay more than 25,000 more through the weekend, according to FlightAware. And more than 1.5 million passengers were stranded.

Faulty technology created the crisis. The FAA’s hamfisted attempts to reassure the public that everything was okay made the situation worse.

For six hours after the ground stop began, the FAA did not provide any public updates except for a terse, 31-word press release and a single X post. Finally, at 11:30PM ET, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to explain the day’s events.

Instead of providing clarity, however, they issued confusing and sometimes even contradictory statements. Mullin opened the conference with a joke (“Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”) before confidently declaring that “there is no cyberattack.” Instead, he appeared to blame the outage on the FAA’s modernization project.

“As Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment and technology was just overwhelming the older system,” said Mullin.

Mullin’s remark appeared to surprise Duffy, who looked at the ground and shook his head. Mullin later walked the statement back after a reporter’s follow-up question, admitting that “there’s nothing completely certain right now.”

Duffy offered more details but did not exactly give a straight answer. “Our switches and routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” he said. “I shouldn’t say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.”

“I don’t want to rule out nefarious activity,” he later added.

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin concluded. “We are built to handle crisis like this.”

A follow-up press conference on Saturday afternoon was equally bizarre. It started with piercing audio feedback produced by a faulty microphone, which interrupted Duffy right after he introduced Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer.

US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy (left) speaks as US Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin listens at the White House after the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights after a major communications outage on November 13th, 2026.

After a four-minute delay, Duffy continued with the briefing. He floated the potential that contractor “incompetence” had caused the outage. And he demanded that Congress allocate billions more dollars to the FAA so it could complete its modernization efforts — calling its existing $12.5 billion modernization budget a “partial payment.”

The conferences only flamed online rumors that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or a rogue AI tied to the September rollout of the FAA’s new SMART system. (So far, no evidence has emerged for either.)

The problem was compounded by an administration already struggling to command public trust. When cabinet officials offered shifting, improvised explanations from the podium, millions of anxious travelers — and even prominent allies — simply refused to take the government at its word.

“Until proven otherwise, not some presser by our government, I firmly believe this was a DDOS attack,” former National Security Adviser Mike Flynn wrote on X. “This is what was being described by two smart cabinet officials who clearly did not understand the technical nature of what happened.”

Khera and her family didn’t know about the political gamesmanship behind the outage — and frankly, they didn’t care. She just wanted to get out of Atlanta on something other than an airplane.

After a night in one of the last available hotel rooms in Atlanta, she and her family rented a car and drove the nine hours back to Virginia Beach. They made it home late Saturday night.

Because of the FAA’s mishaps, they don’t plan to fly again anytime soon.

“We’ve had enough of planes,” she said. “It will take a couple months and more explanations from the FAA to make sure something like this or worse doesn’t happen again.”

Correction, November 16th: L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, not a wireless one. This story has been updated to reflect that fact.
